title: How Much Does Air Duct Cleaning Cost?
h1: How Much Does Air Duct Cleaning Cost, and What Affects the Price?
description: Air duct cleaning cost depends on home size, vent count, attic access and duct condition. Here's what drives the price and how to spot a bait-and-switch deal.
quick_answer: The cost of air duct cleaning depends mostly on how many supply and return vents you have, how big the system is, how easy the attic or closet is to reach and what shape the ducts are in. Add-ons like sanitizing or dryer vent cleaning change the total too. A free on-site estimate gives you a real number.
body:
There's no single price for duct cleaning because no two systems are the same. A small condo with one return and six registers is a very different job from a two-story home with two furnaces and ducts running through a hot attic. What you're really paying for is time, equipment and how much buildup has to come out.

Below are the things that actually move the price, so you can compare quotes on equal terms.

What affects the cost of air duct cleaning?

  • Number of vents. Every supply register and return grille is a run that has to be opened, agitated and vacuumed. More openings means more labor.
  • Number of systems. Larger homes often have two furnaces or air handlers, each with its own trunk lines and returns.
  • Access. Most San Diego and Orange County homes have the furnace in the attic, garage or a hall closet. A cramped attic with low clearance takes longer to work in than an open garage.
  • How dirty the ducts are. A system that hasn't been cleaned in years, or one that went through a remodel without being sealed off, can hold a lot of drywall dust and debris.
  • Duct condition. Older flex duct that's torn, crushed or disconnected may need repair before cleaning makes sense.
  • Add-ons. Sanitizing, cleaning the blower and coil, or adding a dryer vent cleaning to the same visit all affect the final number.

Why do some duct cleaning prices seem so low?

You've probably seen mailers or online ads for whole-house duct cleaning at a price that seems too good to be true. Usually it is. Those offers often cover a light vacuum at each register, and once the crew is inside, the price climbs with add-ons that were never mentioned.

A real cleaning uses a powerful vacuum connected to the system to keep the ducts under negative pressure, plus brushes or air whips to knock buildup loose from the duct walls. That takes a trained crew a good part of the day for a typical home. If a quote doesn't explain what's included, ask before you book.

What should a duct cleaning quote include?

A fair quote should spell out the work so you can compare it with others. Look for:

  • Which supply and return lines are being cleaned, and how many
  • Whether the main trunk lines and plenums are included
  • Whether the blower, coil and return box are cleaned or just inspected
  • The cleaning method and equipment being used
  • Any optional services, priced separately, so you can say yes or no to each one
  • Before and after photos or video so you can see the result

If a company won't commit to what's included until they're standing in your living room, that's a red flag.

Is it worth paying for sanitizing or other add-ons?

Sometimes. Sanitizing makes sense if there's been water damage, a rodent problem, visible mold growth near the system or strong odors. It isn't something every home needs every time. We'd rather explain when it helps than push it on every job.

Dryer vent cleaning is a common add-on because the crew and equipment are already there. If your dryer is taking longer than usual to dry a load, it's worth bundling. Replacing a dirty filter and checking that the filter slot is sealed is also a smart, low-cost step that protects the newly cleaned ducts.

How often do you need to pay for duct cleaning?

Most homes don't need it every year. A good rule is every few years, or sooner if something changes. Things that shorten the cycle in Southern California include:

  • A recent remodel, drywall work or flooring sanding
  • Wildfire smoke that got pulled into the system
  • Pets that shed heavily, or someone in the home with allergies or asthma
  • Rodent activity in the attic near the ducts
  • Moving into a home where you don't know the history

If you change filters on schedule and keep the return area clean, you'll stretch the time between cleanings and get more value from each one.

How do you get an accurate price?

The only way to get a number you can trust is to have someone look at the system. We count the vents, check the attic or closet access, look at duct condition and tell you what we'd recommend and what's optional. Our air duct cleaning estimates are free, and you can check the specials page for any current offers before you book.
faqs: Can I clean my air ducts myself?

You can vacuum register covers and the first few inches of each duct, and you should change your filter regularly. A real cleaning needs a high-powered vacuum that holds the whole system under negative pressure, plus agitation tools that reach deep into the runs. Household vacuums can't do that, and they can stir dust up into the air.
How long does air duct cleaning take?

For a typical single-system home, plan on several hours. Larger homes, two-system homes or heavily soiled ducts take longer. Tight attics also add time, since the crew has to work carefully around insulation and wiring.
Will duct cleaning lower my energy bill?

Clean ducts alone usually won't make a big change on your bill. The bigger savings come from fixing leaks, disconnected runs and a dirty blower or coil, which a good technician will point out during the cleaning.
